dossier.architecture: Low-mass two-joint arm with compact roller claw and specialized side-entry station climb.

subsystems.intake: Three-roller claw for cones and cubes; collect pose rests against a rigid bumper support for repeatability.
subsystems.transfer: Direct claw acquisition, contained within the frame in the collect pose.
subsystems.scoring: Shoulder and elbow transmissions kept near the floor; team reports an approximately 17-pound arm assembly.
subsystems.drivetrain: REV MAXSwerve selected in part for ground clearance and packaging needed by the climb.
subsystems.endgame: Independent powered paws lift the front; underside belts move the robot up the station edge; arm motion completes the sequence.
subsystems.controls: Automated climb sequence and coordinated arm setpoints.

versions: Third competition claw, approximately seventh prototype at filming.
Proposed changes to improve climb repairability were future plans, not established implementations.
dossier.analysis: Study the whole climb/drivetrain package. Copying the paws without the wheel clearance, underside traction and arm motion would omit the mechanism's enabling constraints.
limits: Interview is from the second event; later configurations require separate audit.

context_documents.title: 2023-2046 · Low arm mass and repeatable collect stops support a large reach envelope
context_documents.body:
# 2023-2046: Low arm mass and repeatable collect stops support a large reach envelope

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A lightweight shoulder/elbow arm with low transmissions carries a three-roller claw. The collect pose bears against a rigid bumper support and stays contained. The team reports an approximately 17-pound arm assembly; module selection also considered ground clearance and packaging.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The source explicitly emphasizes reducing mass given the required outward/upward reach and credits Citrus-style claw ideas while making the implementation smaller and lighter. Cube compression is chosen to retain rather than damage the piece.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A mechanical collect stop can define acquisition geometry more repeatably than a high-gain servo alone, provided the bumper/support does not move unpredictably. Reducing distal mass improves torque demand and balance, but must preserve stiffness at maximum reach. Ground-clearance decisions also affect charge-station behavior and any intended special climbing approach.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Measure deflection at full reach, test pickup after bumper displacement, and verify retention across both piece types and abrupt chassis motion.

## Limits

Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

source_reviews.title: 2046 Bear Metal | Behind the Bumpers
source_reviews.review_basis: Read the complete interview publisher introduction.
source_reviews.facts: Publisher identifies side climb, arm, intake and bumper mounts.
source_reviews.limitations: Secondary summary. Full interview captions were unavailable.

source_reviews.title: 2046 interview
source_reviews.review_basis: Inherited synopsis. No fresh full-caption or visual review.
source_reviews.facts: Reports a three-roller direct claw, low transmissions, MAXSwerve, powered paws and underside belts for a station-edge approach.
source_reviews.limitations: Treat specific details and configuration dates as provisional.

source_review.whole_robot_explanation: The Bear Metal dossier describes a light articulated scoring arm and a separate side-entry charge-station mechanism that shares the chassis and arm. The two are coupled by clearance, mass distribution and control sequencing. The scoring tool carries both pieces directly. The endgame description instead calls for the robot to lift its nose with powered paws and use underside traction to advance onto the station. The interview introduction independently confirms the existence of the side climb, arm and intake.
piece_flow: Present the three-roller claw at floor height. The inherited account reports a repeatable collect pose against a bumper support.
Secure the piece in the claw and move both arm joints to the target without an intermediate handoff.
Release at the node and return to a compact posture. The station sequence is separate from the scoring flow.
source_review.packaging_and_motion: The older interview account puts the shoulder and elbow transmissions near the floor, and relates module packaging and ground clearance to the station mechanism. A lower center of mass and less distal inertia help during both travel and repeated arm reversals. The underside clearance has to be checked with bumper compression, drivetrain deflection and station angle included.

subsystems.name: Roller claw and collection stop
subsystems.construction: Older dossier reports three rollers and a hard reference at a bumper support.
subsystems.operation: The tool captures both pieces and retains them through arm motion.
subsystems.team_rationale: The retained account describes a repeatable collection pose and several claw iterations.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: A structural stop can set pickup height reproducibly, provided it takes the load without bending the tool or unloading the wheels.
subsystems.interfaces: The stop and bumper mount share the collection interface. An impact to either can shift contact geometry.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Check unloaded and loaded pickup height after a bumper change. Inspect rollers and the stop for off-axis wear.
subsystems.unknowns: Roller geometry, stop material and actual prototype sequence.

subsystems.name: Two-joint arm
subsystems.construction: Older dossier reports low-mounted transmissions and a team-described arm assembly of roughly 17 pounds.
subsystems.operation: Coordinated setpoints place the direct tool at grid heights. The arm reportedly also moves in the station sequence.
subsystems.team_rationale: The older account characterizes a low-mass architecture. Exact mass boundary is unclear.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Low actuator placement helps mass distribution but requires transmitting torque to the moving joint. Check phase, backlash and loaded tip deflection.
subsystems.interfaces: The loaded arm changes chassis pitch and support reactions. The station mechanism may depend on a specific arm pose.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Check wiring and lost position after contact. Test a safe intermediate recovery if movement stops halfway.
subsystems.unknowns: Ratios, arm mass boundary, sensing and interlocks.

subsystems.name: Side-entry station hardware
subsystems.construction: Older dossier reports powered paws, underside belts and MAXSwerve selected in part for clearance.
subsystems.operation: Paws raise the front, underside belts advance the chassis, and arm motion completes the sequence according to the retained account.
subsystems.team_rationale: The older synopsis reports a specialized station approach and proposed repairability changes.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Map the center of mass against successive support contacts. A successful initial lift does not establish enough traction or stability for the transition to the deck.
subsystems.interfaces: Wheel and bumper clearance, left/right paw timing, belt traction and arm pose are part of one path.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Test asymmetrical contact, low traction and safe retreat after a stalled transition. Assess access to replace a paw or belt.
subsystems.unknowns: Contact geometry, actuation and later event installations.

revisions: Older dossier records the third competition claw at filming and proposed climb service changes. Proposed changes are unverified.
transferable_principles: Prototype the complete support transition with representative bumpers and mass, and measure recovery from a missed contact.
disconfirming_conditions: Transfer fails when the edge profile, friction or partner clearance removes a reliable support transition. A simpler standard approach can also erase the side approach's marginal value.
remaining_gaps: Full captions or team hardware write-up, contact-sequence timing and later revisions.
recommended_images: Seek an underside view and a side sequence showing paw, belt and wheel contacts.
